docs/rules-reference.md |     - **It finishes rivals off.** When a rival is down to a handful of territories (6 or fewer, or a tenth of its own, and it holds at least three times as much; {}; not in the opening's first 14 turns), it goes and ends them: recruits at the sites nearest them, marches troops through its own land (one order a hop) to every territory next to theirs, strikes their armies first with half as much again as it takes (counting what they could recruit before the strike lands; Seize the Initiative on the biggest), chains on through the rest of their land and the empty land they could run to, keeps every territory next to their armies strong enough to hold, and brings spare troops up for next turn. Once it holds 75% of the map it treats every rival that way (as **Clean up** does, §14). A strike that's ready before anyone can move goes first in its queue. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md |     - **The Blitzer:** expands as fast as it can and chains everything; builds nothing and defends little. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md |     - **The Turtle:** forts, culture and markets first; takes only safe land and attacks rivals only with a big edge until turn 14, then strikes. | semicolon

Then it proposes a **joint war** against it at once, for 6 turns, and again as soon as one ends; every Marshal accepts one; its fronts with the runaway come first. | dash

docs/rules-reference.md |   - **Its budget** is paid in each turn as income comes in: **a share of the turn's income** (after upkeep; rounded down) or **an exact amount** (up to 99 gold a turn). Budgets are paid in order (your Leader, your Steward, then captured ones) and never more than your treasury holds. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md |   - **On screen:** your missions are on your Leader card with their deadline; tap one to light its target up on the map. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md |   - **Personalities** (each game deals them from its seed, no two the same until all six are used; hidden while you play, revealed at the end, or shown all along with "Show personalities" in the lobby). Style only: every one plays by the same rules and gold. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md |   - **Siege engines** cut the fort's bonus as ever; they don't cut the shared defenders. **Walls never attack:** a walled army attacks with its own troops. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md |   - **The sweep covers the fog** (session 20d, Nate's third note). Its set is everywhere the remnant **is** (what you see and remember of theirs), **might be** (land you've never seen at all, and land in the fog within 2 steps of theirs, or of never-seen land, that was empty, theirs or yours when you last saw it: they could have taken it since; land a third House held stays that House's as far as you know), and **could move to** (their armies' reach). The fogged parts take their turn by distance like the rest (they used to be visited last). **More chains:** what the first chains didn't reach is swept by more, from the spare troops left, strongest first, each from the territory of yours next to it that can gather the most within 3 steps. The blanket also covers your land next to where they might be. Every hop attacks only if still stronger, so nothing in the fog is attacked blind: the engine checks the real odds when it plays. Settings: {} (2) and {}. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md |   - **Walls up fast:** the fort first (it takes two turns to build), then as many levels of culture as the purse holds, in the same turn. With 40 gold a Steward takes your capital from culture 0 to 5 and starts its fort in one turn (31 + 8 gold); the wall stands when the fort does, at the end of the next turn. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md |   - **What every Marshal does** (whatever its personality): it **attacks hard**, chaining on whenever the next hop is likely to win, up to 6 hops, and throws every spare troop in; it doesn't hold troops back on quiet fronts (it still holds choke points, a threatened capital and its fronts with a runaway); it **expands hardest in the first 14 turns**; it goes for **whole provinces** (land that would complete one is worth more); and it prefers to **end a chain on defensible ground** (where few open borders face it). | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md |   - **What it learned in session 19:** it queues troops first, then its armies' moves, then everything else it buys (each order takes a round, so a purchase queued first lets rivals move first); it doesn't hire cavalry on a whim; and it keeps a **guard at its capital**: half of the biggest rival army it knows of within 3 steps, and for the first 3 turns half its own stack (capitals on Embervale are 3 steps apart: without the guard, 14% of Marshals were knocked out on turn 1). A Leader you put on "Run the military" keeps the same guard. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md |   - **What it learned in session 20c** (Nate's second note; your leaders do all of this too): | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md |   - At most 2 missions open; a third draw becomes an event. A mission lapses at its deadline, or the moment you lose the land you were to hold. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md |   - The Turtle and the Merchant keep their order of things inside the plan (the Turtle walls before its markets; the Merchant buys its markets first). The Marshal's own building keeps session 20b's way for now (session 22 looks at the Marshal adopting it). | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md |   4. **Sweep:** from there one chain strikes their army and walks on through **everywhere they are and everywhere their armies could get to this turn** (worked out from each army's strength against what stands in its way, and from their recruit sites: their capital, a barracks, a province they hold whole, or one whose land you've never seen), nearest first, back through your own land where it must, and on into unseen land that joins theirs; your Leader on it. An army too big to strike yet is struck only once it has marched out (each hop attacks only if still stronger), and the chain follows its trail. With what's left it goes on to the other remnants' land. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | **Keys** (session 20, Nate): with an attack, move or path box open, **Enter** confirms it exactly as shown (the amount, the Leader going or staying, Initiative or Wait as set, the way picked) and **Esc** cancels it; the buttons are still there for changing anything first. In a leader's command menu, the arrow keys move the highlight and Enter picks the command. Keys never interrupt typing (a leader's name, an exact amount) or a shortcut held with Ctrl, Alt or Shift. On a laptop the confirm button shows a small **↵**; a phone has no keyboard, so it doesn't. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md | *A 10-minute read. This is how the engine actually plays today. Numbers are the current balance settings from {}; they will change as we tune.* | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Binding:** each side pays gold up front, more for longer and bigger deals. The game won't let you queue an attack across it (the order panel says why), and any attack that would cross it the turn it starts is called off with a line in the report. Gold owed each turn is taken automatically; if you're short, troops desert for it as with upkeep. It can't be broken. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Bots:** the Captain gives open missions a modest pull: an attack that would complete one scores a little higher (×1.3), but only among attacks it already judged likely to win; it builds a mission's fort or raises its culture only with gold to spare. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md | - **Caps:** never on a capital; never takes a player's last territory or knocks anyone out; at most one Fate event per territory a turn; culture protects (§7). | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Culture is lost when land changes hands** (session 16, Nate): a captured territory drops to **culture 0** for its new owner; so does land traded in a deal, or taken by rebels. **Buildings stay** (a fort keeps standing for the new owner). Culture is an investment in land you mean to keep. The territory card says so on someone else's land ("Lost if you take it"), and the report says when a capture wiped some out. (The share kept is {}, 0.) | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Defaults:** your **Steward starts on "Run the realm" with 20% of your income** (session 19: **10% on a crowded table**, 12 or fewer territories a player, such as Embervale with 4 or more or Greatmarch with 8–10, where buildings pay back too slowly for more), so building and culture happen even if you never open the Leaders panel. "Run the realm" buys urgent forts, markets, a barracks where needed, culture where it protects, and (session 19) culture for its income where a level pays back as well as a market. Your **Leader starts with no command and no budget**: you order its army yourself, as before. | dash

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Diplomacy: On / Off** is a lobby switch next to the Fate deck's (on by default; Nate, session 15). Off means no Propose, no offers and no deals: every House fights alone, and the bots play exactly as they did before diplomacy. The setting is part of the game, so a save keeps it. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Fair seats (sessions 19 and 20b):** among equal bots some capital spots won far more often than others on every map. So the layouts for each official map's suggested table sizes were checked by simulation, and 14 were replaced by fairer ones the simulator found (Embervale 4 in session 19; 13 more in 20b: {}, "Fair seats"). Most maps still have a weaker spot; a start bonus for it is listed for Nate, not built. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Fully zoomed out, the whole map is clear of the menus** (desktop: the top bar, the map buttons, the right column, the selected-territory panel and the dock; phone: the top bar, the action bar and an open sheet). You can pan any edge of the map into the clear part at every zoom. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Hand limit 5:** at 5 cards you must turn in a set that turn (five cards always hold one). The sensible set is already first in your queue when the turn starts (one of each, else Swords, else a fort where you're most threatened, else Laurels at home); change it or delete it if you like. If no set goes in, the game turns one in for you as the turn ends. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Handshake:** free. You can break one, by attacking across it, missing a payment, or making a truce with your joint war's target. Breaking it brings a public **Oathbreaker** mark for 5 turns, a gold fine and unrest (troops desert from your land next to the player you wronged; culture protects as usual). All three scale with the deal's size: how much land it covers, how long it runs, how much it trades; "until X is knocked out" counts as big. **The fine is 4 gold + 1.4 per point of size, and up to 0.8 troops per point desert** (Nate doubled both in session 15). A truce everywhere for 3 turns over 6 territories (size 9) costs about 17 gold and 7 troops. The offer card says it in plain words: "Handshake: free. Breaking it brings the Oathbreaker mark, about 17 gold and unrest." | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Hire** a spy at your capital or a barracks (in Spend, next to the specialists): **8 gold**. **Upkeep only while it's away** (session 16, Nate): nothing while it stays in your own land (at home, or guarding a province you hold), **1 gold a turn** while it's travelling (sent somewhere) or inside land you don't hold (paid with your specialists; if you can't pay, troops desert as with any upkeep; {} and {}). You may have **up to 5**. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **How it looks** (session 21, the polish pass): the replay is letterboxed with a soft vignette and a warmer light; armies march as the House's soldiers with their banner (ships on sea lanes) behind an inked campaign line, and meet **at the border**, where the fight is (dust, smoke, sparks, the defenders' arrows, a Siege stone); a capture topples the old banner and raises the new one; a capital falling gets smoke, flames and a gentle push-in of the camera. Building, culture, Spoils, Fate, the Fallen, deals and your spies each have a short signature. None of it changes what happened: the numbers, results and pop-ups say the same as before, and the fog still shows only the soft pulse. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **How it plays (the sims, {}; session 20d in {}):** since session 20d your Steward walls in about three games in four, from about turn 13, several territories a game. Those walls are attacked about once a game on the big maps and nearly always fall to that attack (a Marshal attacks a wall only when it's sure, counting the garrison), so a wall's real work is the attacks it puts off. Game length and runaways are the same with walls on and off. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Influence:** you start with 8 ({}); each of the Fallen earns 1 Influence a turn, plus 0.5 for each other Fallen player. Several Fallen aiming the same event at the same place pool their Influence. Putting more than the cost toward an event makes it stronger, up to 1.5 times. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Knocked-out bots are Fallen bots** (§16), whatever their level (the Fallen see the whole political map, so they don't need the Marshal's estimates): on their **first turn out they strike whoever holds the most land** with what they can afford (session 19); after that they aim world events at whoever looks to be leading, by the same runaway rule as priority 8, judged from their political map. With fewer than three players left, they aim at the leader once it holds 1.25 times the land of the next. They pick, best first: an uprising in the leader's quietest land, a plague where it holds the most of a province, a famine, mercenaries next to its land that borders neutral land, a storm on its border with another player. Every Fallen bot judges the same way, so they often pool. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Land on the way that changed hands** when the order comes up: the army stops at your last territory before it (if there is one on the way; otherwise the order doesn't go). The report says so. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Land:** your first 10 territories are free; after that, upkeep climbs faster than your land does (0.35 × extra territories^1.25, rounded). This is the main brake on runaway leaders. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Limits:** every deal ends after 8 turns at most. One deal of each kind between the same two players at a time. When a player is knocked out, their deals end; the Fallen don't make deals. A leader can't be told to raid a partner. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Map shapes and sizes (session 10):** the map maker can now make island chains (every island joined by sea lanes), twin continents, land ringing an inland sea, a crescent, or land in a silhouette (a dragon, a shield, a crown), from 40 to 120 territories, with provinces sized to match and fair capitals for every player count a map claims. Candidates are in {}; none is in the lobby until Nate picks. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md | - **Marshal (hard, the default; session 17):** the Captain's priorities below, with what the simulator found wins, and a personality. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md | - **Numbers:** {}. Spies don't make games longer, and leave runaways and seat fairness where they were; one spy about pays for itself. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **On screen:** a grey stone wall round the outside of each wall's whole footprint, standing up off the land, with the House's glow round it; from Mid zoom in, battlements and square towers at its corners and along long stretches, each flying a pennant in the House colour (Nate's picture). A wall you only remember is greyed like a remembered building. Drawn in code until a painted wall piece comes in an art batch. Before you buy the last piece, the culture and build panels say "Completes a wall". The report says when land becomes walled. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **On screen:** a small card stack with its count on your Leader card (on a phone, by the map buttons), saying "Collect three: three alike, or one of each (best)". Tap it, then a set: 2 taps. The Spoils sheet always shows the table above, with the sets your hand can make lit; one of each comes first, with chips to pick its building (a fort unless you pick another). A building, fort or culture goes on the territory you have selected if it can. The report says what a set gave ("You turned in one of each: a market at Galeholt, 6 troops (4 at Ashfell, 2 at Ravenmoor) and 10 gold"). The stack glows red when your hand is full. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **On screen:** the **Leaders panel** (laptop: the right column; phone: the Leaders sheet, from your Leader's portrait by the map buttons) lists every leader with its portrait, name, kind, what it's doing, its purse and budget, and how many orders it wrote this turn. Tap one for **Command**, **Budget** (chips: 0, 10, 20, 30, 50%, or an exact amount) and **Take back**. While a leader is open, its command shows on the map: the target glows and the provinces it works in get a gold band. The top bar shows your treasury, and the purses' total beside it, smaller. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Pause** (single player, session 13): with a timer on, the round button next to it stops the clock and the timer reads **Paused**. You can keep planning while it's paused (the map dims a little so you notice); nothing locks in until you resume, and the clock carries on from where it stopped. Without a timer there's no button. (Online games will pause by vote, in M4.) | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Personalities** (session 20c, Nate): next to your Leader's name in the lobby, one tap picks **Neutral** (the default: the balanced way, as before), **the Conqueror** (picks one front and masses there), **the Blitzer** (never stops a chain short, never pulls back), **the Opportunist** (goes for whoever just fought) or **the Schemer** (picks off the weakened); next to your Steward's, **Neutral**, **the Turtle** (forts wherever an army of 3 or more stands next door, and up to 3 levels of culture a turn where they protect, before markets) or **the Merchant** (markets first, then the urgent forts, then culture for its income). Remembered on your device like the names. A leader with a personality plans with that Marshal personality's weights and switches ({}) under its command; it **keeps its personality for life**, including when captured. The Leaders panel says "Aldric, the Conqueror", and the report and the Chronicle give it a line in its own voice when it took land ("Aldric, the Conqueror: “Took Ashfell and Pinemark; Morwen's lot ran.”"). A Neutral leader says nothing and plays exactly as before. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Saves never leave the device.** If the browser can't store them (a private window, storage switched off, a full disk), you get a plain message and the game goes on; Save to a file still works. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Seeing their orders:** they're written into your order queue as planning starts, each with its leader's portrait, and you can change or delete any of them. **"Leaders' orders: Mixed in / After mine"** (in Settings, and at the top of the queue; mixed in by default) chooses where they play: one of yours, then one of theirs, or all of yours first. If the timer runs out, they go in as they are. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Settings → Effects: Full / Light / Off** (remembered on the device). Light halves the particles and drops the camera shake and flashes; Off keeps only the information (armies' numbers, battles, results, pop-ups). A phone that can't keep the replay smooth on Full moves to Light by itself and says so once; "Reduce motion" on the device starts on Light. The replay's length doesn't depend on the setting. | arrow

Light halves the particles and drops the camera shake and flashes; Off keeps only the information (armies' numbers, battles, results, pop-ups). docs/rules-reference.md | - **Shared defenders:** when a walled territory is attacked, **every other territory of its wall** (at any distance along it, Nate's call; {}) lends its **spare troops** (all but the 1 that holds its land; {}) to the defence. Nate's example: three walled territories with 4 troops each, one attacked: **the attacker faces 10**. The attacked territory's terrain, fort, culture and Leader count for all of them. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Spies act between turns**, after every army's move: a called-home spy is back at your capital as the next turn starts; the others travel **2 territories** toward the province you sent them to. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Spread over your front:** one troop at a time to whichever of your territories is worst off (the biggest rival army next door, less what's there and what it's been given so far); with no rival next to you, the land facing neutral land; with none, your capital. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **The Chronicle** is a log of every turn so far: battles you saw, Fate events (yours, those on your land, those you saw, and "something stirs" in the fog), the Fallen's events, deals made, broken and ended, your spies' news, and your leaders' work. Newest turn first; in each turn, what touched you first. A switch shows only what touched you. **Tap a line to see the place on the map.** | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **The awards**, each with the winner's portrait: **Best Military** (most battles won: land taken plus attacks held off), **Best Culture** (most culture raised), **Master Builder** (most buildings finished), **Spymaster** (most spies into a rival's province), **Diplomat** (most deals kept to the end), **Survivor** (of everyone but the winner, who held out longest), and **Iron Wall** (most attacks held off), **Kingslayer** (most rival Leaders felled), **Fortune's Favourite** (most good Fate on their land), **Quartermaster** (most troops recruited) and **Oathbreaker** (most handshake deals broken). Ties are shared; an award nobody earned isn't given. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **The bigger maps (session 19, Nate's OK):** **Ashwing** (a phoenix, 160 territories, suits 6–8), **The Sundered Crowns** (twin continents, 160, suits 6–8), **Krakenmere** (a kraken, 200, suits 8–10) and **Rootholm** (a tree of life, 200, suits 8–10). The lobby shows a line under the map choice saying who each map suits and what it plays like. Details: {}. | dash

docs/rules-reference.md | - **The bots:** your Steward on Run the realm walls with a plan (session 20d, §14): forts on choke points and wall candidates, the wall up fast (several culture levels in a turn), everything into it when you're threatened; your Leader keeps 4 troops in walled land facing a rival. (Build up this province still finishes a wall where a territory worth holding needs at most 18 gold more, session 20b's way.) The Marshal builds walls in its own style (the Turtle from scratch, the Blitzer never; only on roomy tables, where it builds like the Steward). The Captain and the Recruit don't. Every bot counts a wall's garrison when it attacks, and its own walls' lenders when it guards. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **The lobby (session 17):** Recruit (easy), Captain (medium), **Marshal (hard, the default)**, or **Mixed**: choose how many Marshals with − and + ("2 Marshals and 3 Captains"); they're seated at random. A saved game keeps each bot's level, personality and memory. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **The power graph:** each House's share of the map, turn by turn, from the start. One line per House in its colour, with its banner's pattern as the line's dash (so you can tell Houses apart without colour) and the winner's line strongest; names at the ends of the lines (on a phone, the winner's), a legend, a readout as you move along it, and the numbers as a table. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **The re-confirm rule:** a deal starts only if both sides confirm during the same planning phase. It starts as the turn plays, **before any move**. An offer nobody confirmed lapses as the turn plays; one between two players who fought each other that turn is void. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **They keep their word,** except the Captain may break a handshake deal for a rival's capital it's sure to take (or the win, with fog off), when the gain is at least twice the penalty, and it says so in the report. With the harsher Oathbreaker that now happens mostly with small deals (a truce on a few borders); a 3-turn truce everywhere is usually kept even for a capital. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **They never hoard** (session 20; session 20d, Nate's third note): a leader with a military command spends its whole purse on troops (and the specialists and barracks it needs) every turn it can recruit anywhere. Recruits are shared out across the sites that need them, and a recruit whose site is lost before it runs **tries up to four other sites of yours** in turn, the safest first (any of yours: the troops are still the leader's to march). The only reason it keeps gold is one it names in the panel ("Saving 4 gold: nowhere to recruit until the barracks at Galeholt is up"); with nowhere at all to recruit it builds that barracks as soon as it can pay for it (6 gold). An odd gold coin it can't spend (a troop costs 2) waits in the purse for next turn. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **They write as many orders as the realm needs** (session 20): finishing a rival, a Leader on Run the military writes a march for every hop through your land, a strike for every territory of theirs, and the chains on (dozens a turn on a big map); it matches or beats a Marshal planning the same seat on 9 turns in 10. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Up to 4 of each kind, your own included** ({}). Take over two players and you command three military leaders and three Stewards. With one too many, you choose who goes; if you don't, the military leaders nearest your front stay, and the Stewards with the most in their purses. A leader let go sends its purse home. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **What players see:** the holder of the land always sees the event. Others see it in full only if they can see the land; otherwise only "something stirs in Northreach" (whoever drew it too). | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md | - **Where:** the Chronicle button in the top bar (desktop); the scroll button with the map buttons (phone). | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Your Leader goes with the army** (session 16). An attack or move from where your Leader stands takes it along **by default** (+20%); one tap on **Stays home**, right on the attack panel, leaves it behind. It **carries on through a chain**: each hop you add from where it should arrive takes it on too, and so does **Follow through**. If an attack fails, it falls back with the survivors; if the army is wiped out, it falls (and comes back next turn, §9). The report says "with N troops and your Leader". | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Your Steward** runs culture, buildings, forts and the economy. It never stands on the map and can't be lost. Naming it is optional; left blank, it gets a name from the game's seed. Until Steward portraits are made, it shows as your House's shield with a quill. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | - **Your orders come first:** an order of yours out of a territory takes that army back from its leader for the turn (a leader leading just its own army, on Hold, Defend, Push or Raid, steps aside altogether); a build or culture of yours on a place takes that place back from your Steward. Seize the Initiative and Lie in Wait stay yours. | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md | - A knocked-out player's own captured leaders are gone with them; only their own two pass on. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | It says what it adds ("7 orders: take 6 territories, end at Old March"), and Confirm adds exactly that many. **Confirm** puts the orders in your queue as one chain of ordinary hops (each sends All and attacks only if still stronger; your Leader goes along if it starts with the army), so you can change or delete any step. It walks through your own land and land taken earlier on the path (moves), marches through a partner's land you have right of passage through (at most 3 territories in one move), and **never attacks the land of anyone you have a truce or joint war with**. It plans only from what you see and remember: land you've never seen counts as lightly held. On a phone: 4 taps for the shortest way, 5 for the full sweep. | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | | **Expand our empire in this direction** (Nate's) | Pick a target territory. It commands its own army and yours in the provinces on the way. Through empty, weak land it chains fast; where rival armies stand it's careful (only where what arrives would hold, with honest garrisons behind it); it takes and secures whole provinces on the way rather than a thin line. At the target it stops and holds. | 4 | | semicolon
docs/rules-reference.md | | **Move / attack** | Send troops to a neighbouring territory. If it's yours, they move in; if not, they attack. You choose **how many** as a share (below). | | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | | **Push back <rival>** (session 20, Nate) | Pick a rival: it takes that rival's weakly held land (the less there, the better), breaking its chains, keeps clear of its big armies until it can beat them, and never touches anyone else (empty land only on the way to theirs; never a partner). It commands its own army and yours facing that rival. One plain reason a turn in the panel ("Going for Pinemark; Baron Krell's main army at Galeholt (40) is too big for now"). | 4 | | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | | **Recruit** | Buy troops (2 gold each) at your capital, any barracks, or **any territory in a province you hold completely** (session 9). Choose how many with the same chips as attacks: All, 3/4, 1/2 or 1/4 of your gold (an exact number under More; the default is All). You can queue several recruits to split troops across sites, and edit them in the queue. While Recruit is open, every place you can recruit glows. Ask for more than you can afford and you get as many as you can pay for. New troops can act the same turn. | | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | | **Run the realm** | Builds with a plan (session 20d, below): markets and barracks deep inside the realm, forts on choke points and where walls will go, the wall up fast when you're threatened. Urgent forts first (a threatened capital, choke points facing an army); it saves up for an urgent fort rather than buy lesser things. Only one Steward at a time. | 4 | | semicolon

docs/rules-reference.md | | **Trade** | Gold now, gold each turn (for up to 5 turns), or land (up to 3 territories in a deal, never a capital or land with a Leader in it; it must border the other side's land). The giver's troops there step back to its own strongest neighbouring territory, one of the receiver's troops moves in from its strongest neighbouring army, and buildings stay with the land (its culture is lost, §7). A trade with nothing paid each turn is done at once. | | semicolon
